The Final Shift: Beeshoek

By: Anina Peens | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A town built on iron now stands on hope alone

Unique Selling Point:
As South Africa’s industrial heart falls silent, one small mining community on the edge of the Kalahari faces a reckoning: what happens to a town when the mine that built it begins to fade?

Summary:
On the edge of the Kalahari lies Beeshoek, a mining town built on red earth and iron ore and on the life that grew around its heartbeat, the mine club. For decades, the Ammosal Club was where miners celebrated paydays, children learned to swim, and families gathered under the floodlights after long shifts underground. It was the soul of a community sustained by the mine’s rhythm.
Now, that rhythm is faltering. As South Africa’s steel industry declines and ArcelorMittal slows production, Beeshoek’s future and the life built around it hangs in the balance. The ore that once forged the nation’s pride now sails east to feed foreign furnaces, returning as imported steel at a price South Africans can no longer afford.

Further information:
A drone rises above the dust of the Northern Cape. The town of Postmasburg stretches small and thin across the landscape, its streets quiet, its future uncertain. On a map it barely registers, just another dot in a wide, arid land. But for the people who live here, the world has always begun and ended in one place, the Beeshoek mine.
For the workers, the mine was more than an employer. It was a father, a constant presence. At sixteen you left school, and your path was already set. Your hands would carry ore, as your father’s had, as your grandfather’s had before him. Generations lined up against the horizon of the pit, their lives defined by shifts and sirens.
This is where it began, ninety-nine years ago. A handful of workers and their families, bound together by the earth.
The clubhouse became its second heartbeat, established around the rugby club, Ammosal. It became well-known for producing 4 Springbok rugby players, and scores of Griekwa players. The club became the life of the community. It is such a culture, such a core of who they were that the Springboks who came from here, had their ashes scattered on the rugby field.
And now, the mine will not turn 100 years old next year. It is closing its doors before Christmas leaving behind generations of families who know no life beyond mining. Their story unfolds against the backdrop of South Africa’s collapsing steel industry.
The closure of Beeshoek is not an isolated tragedy, but the symptom of a far wider collapse. South Africa’s government has failed to regulate and protect its steel industry, allowing cheap imports and weak oversight to hollow out local production. At the same time, the collapse of Transnet’s rail network has crippled the movement of ore, forcing mines to rely on costly, inefficient road transport that eats away at margins. Layered over this is Eskom’s spiraling energy crisis: power cuts that stall production, soaring tariffs that push costs beyond viability, and an unreliable grid that makes long-term planning impossible. The story of Postmasburg is therefore more than a community losing its heartbeat, it is a warning of how national policy failure, broken infrastructure, and a failing power utility are dismantling the backbone of South Africa’s industrial economy.
Shutdowns & Layoff Plans
• AMSA (ArcelorMittal South Africa) is preparing to shut its long steel operations in Newcastle and Vereeniging.
• Initially, about 3,500 job cuts were expected from those closures. But unions now warn the cuts could escalate to 4,000 employees, nearly half of AMSA’s workforce, as the layoffs expand to include the Vanderbijlpark flat-steel operations.
• In Newcastle, the blast furnace has been placed into care and maintenance, a transitional state often used before full closure.
• AMSA had previously deferred the final shutdown to 30 September, backed by funding from the Industrial Development Corporation (IDC).

THE FINAL SHIFT: BEESHOEK final script
(Govan subtitles) Good morning.
(Shop Assistant subtitles) Good morning, sir. How are you?
(Govan subtitles) I’m good thank you. Can I please have a sandwich with egg and bacon and coffee?
(Shop Assistant subtitles) Certainly.
(Govan) Breakfast in a town at the edge of the Kalahari.
(Shop Assistant subtitles) Here you go, sir.
(Govan subtitles) Thank you.
(Shop Assistant subtitles) Enjoy it.
(Govan subtitles) Thanks very much, Bianca.
(Govan) The Northern Cape town of Postmasburg, about 170km from Upington, owes much of its existence to a nearby mine called Beeshoek. In the 100 years since its establishment, it’s grown into a close-knit community. And mining will forever be at its heart, or so the people living here thought.

(Leonie horn subtitles) Because Beeshoek is such an old mine, and so deeply woven into history, it’s literally become like a father to the town, they’re seen as one and the same. Postmasburg can’t exist without Beeshoek, and Beeshoek can’t exist without Postmasburg.
(Govan) But events thousands of kms away, in Joburg boardrooms and the iron ore smelters of the Vaal triangle and northern KZN, are jeopardising that existence. The global steel industry is under financial strain, with multinational manufacturers cutting operations.
(Adèle Rossouw subtitles) If we want to be angry, we should channel that anger toward the government that failed to intervene, because this didn’t happen overnight. The decay has been years in the making.
(Govan) So, we visited Postmasburg to see how life is changing in a town facing a future without Beeshoek mine.
(Archive sportscaster) It’s a legend, its rivet, its raucous it is Grikwas.
(Govan) This year, Griquas won the Currie Cup for the first time since 1970.
(Wilna Koen subtitles) When Griquas last won the Currie Cup, three-quarters of the players were Ammosal players who ran out for the team.

(Govan) Ammosal is Beeshoek Mine’s rugby club. Founded in 1929, it’s produced some of the sport’s most famous names.

(Govan) Wilna Koen is the club’s manager and oversees its collection of memorabilia.
(Wilna Koen subtitles) Those are the four rugby players who came from the Ammosal Rugby Club. The four Springboks were Piet Visagie, Piet van Deventer, Joggie Viljoen, and Kobus Rooiland. Which other club can say it’s had four players in its history who became Springboks?
(Govan) Beeshoek’s first mine manager was a man called Jambo Harris, who was as passionate about rugby as he was about mining.
(Wilna Koen subtitles) So this is where old Colonel Jambo Harris always sat. This is his chair, no one sits on it because it’s Colonel Jambo Harris’s chair.
(Govan subtitles) He looks like a strict man.
(Wilna Koen subtitles) He was a very strict man, he came from the army.
(Govan) Jumbo’s story illustrates perfectly the shaping of a town based on its connection to a mine and its love of rugby.
(Wilna Koen subtitles) Jumbo Harris’s passion was rugby, so he brought in people from far and wide, if you could play good rugby, even better, he’d recruit you to the Beeshoek Club and give you a good job here.
(Govan subtitles) They were rugby players first, and miners second.
(Wilna Koen subtitles) Yes, when you came for the interview, he’d ask you, what position do you play?
(Govan) Piet Visagie, who made his Springbok debut in 1967, was one such recruit.
(Govan subtitles) He was a mine worker?
(Wilna Koen subtitles) He was a mine worker, he was the payroll master, and many times he also drove the school bus to take the children to school. In 2022, Piet Visagie died. In 2023 his family came to scatter his ashes here on the rugby field.
(Leonie Horn subtitles) They were really famous, I mean, they were heroes.
(Govan) Leonie Horn is Beeshoek’s current mine manager.

(Leonie Horn subtitles) Beeshoek is very special to me. I spent my entire high school career here.
(Govan subtitles) What does the red dust mean to you?
(Leonie Horn subtitles) This isn’t the red Kalahari sand with dunes that you know, this is iron ore, so it’s dirty, it’s oily. It makes everything red, the cars are red, your clothes are red. We had a white cat once, and when people came to visit, the lady asked, what do you use to dye the cat? We said, No, it’s the sand, that’s why he’s pink.
(Govan) Leoni’s father was Beeshoek’s head engineer in the 80’s and 90’s and she took over as mine manager from her sister.

(Leonie Horn subtitles) Even my grandfather and my uncles and aunts worked on the mine. It becomes part of you; it’s in your genes. I got married in the Reformed Church in Postmasburg, and the reception was held here in the hall.
(Govan subtitles) On the mine!
(Govan) Globally, the steel industry is under massive pressure, Among other factors, there’s an almost constant over-supply which keeps prices depressed. After peaking four years ago, the industry’s financial performance has collapsed to historic lows. And towns built to support the industry are feeling the impact. In Newcastle, northern KZN, steel multi-national ArcelorMittal, also known as AMSA, has announced the biggest mass retrenchments in the country’s history. Formerly known as Iscor, the smelter once created thousands of jobs, but it’s now buckling from the pressure of rising electricity costs and cheap steel imports. AMSA is Beeshoek’s only client.
(Andrè Joubert) Amsa is the last real steel producer in South Africa and because the economy is not growing, they can’t make steel profitable anymore. Because they can’t make steel profitable, they don’t buy ore from us and we’ve got no other option but to close the mine down.
(Govan) Andre Joubert oversees iron ore operations for African Rainbow Minerals, a major shareholder in Beeshoek. He says the mine is preparing for its final shift.

(Andrè Joubert) The last 18 months, this mine and the contract with Amsa was a month-on-month contract. And in July, I did not have a contract for August and we still continued to mine in good faith we kept on going.
(Govan) In the past four months, the mine has produced nearly 900 THOUSAND tons of ore… but they can’t get it to market.
(Govan) Is there a market to sell the ore that you have taken out here?
(Andrè Joubert) Absolutely.
(Govan) where is that market?
(Andrè Joubert) In China.
(Govan) what is stopping the access to the market that is over there?
(Andrè Joubert) Transnet, I cannot get the ore from here, onto the railway line to Saldana to export.
(Adèle Rossouw subtitles) Every time you spot an unfamiliar bakkie outside Beeshoek, you hope it’s a buyer.
(Govan) Adèle Rossouw, from the Trade Union, Solidarity, is doing all she can to save jobs at Beeshoek. Adele takes us to a quiet suburb where many of Beeshoek’s miners live.
(Adèle Rossouw subtitles) The houses are so beautiful to me, and that’s why I wanted us to stop here, so you can see what the mine did. They helped people become homeowners. The reality is that by December or January, all the families with children in school who have to relocate, there’s going to be a big move-out by the end of the year.
(Govan Subtitles) Out of this neighbourhood? It’s such a nice area, kids ride their bikes here.
(Adèle Rossouw subtitles) Yes, it’s moms and dads losing their jobs. Those children will have to move and find new schools.
(Govan) If that happens, as seems likely, it’ll mean the younger generations will lose a connection to Beeshoek and its legacy.
(Adèle Rossouw subtitles) It’s always such a beautiful story for me, when you ask the children here in Postmasburg what they want to be one day, they say, “a multiskilled operator.” It’s so humble such a modest dream.
(Govan subtitles) In Postmasburg, being a multiskilled operator is a badge of honour from Beeshoek
(Adèle Rossouw subtitles) If we want to be angry, we should channel that anger toward the government. Beeshoek lost its only client, and the reason is total state collapse. Why did Amsa collapse? It’s because of corruption, electricity issues, and all the problems with Transnet. These job losses are a bloodbath.
(Leonie Horn subtitles) Everyone is being retrenched, it’s a full retrenchment even I’m being retrenched. We’ve really looked at everything, we’ve tried everything. We even tried things they told us wouldn’t work, but we did it anyway, just so we could say we tried.
(Govan) But this is not a community that easily surrenders hope. And there’s no better monument to its fighting spirit than the sports club at the centre of life at the mine.
(Wilna Koen Subtitles) When we got the news that things were going to be stopped, I cried at first because I told myself, I don’t k now how I’ll lock the front door behind me for the last time. I’ll fight until the day I walk out of here to make sure this history is preserved, for our children and for those who remain behind.
(Adèle Rossouw subtitles) For the next 36 months, if Beeshoek reopens, the people can be called back.
(Govan subtitles) Well, at least there’s that.
(Adèle Rossouw subtitles) I think that little flame of hope is still burning in everyone’s hearts.
(Govan) And as they wait, perhaps they can find inspiration in a team of underdogs who defied the odds to be crowned provincial rugby champions for the first time in more than 50 years.

(Leonie Horn subtitles) Even my grandfather and my uncles and aunts worked on the mine. It becomes part of you; it’s in your genes. I got married in the Reformed Church in Postmasburg, and the reception was held here in the hall. (Govan subtitles) On the mine! (Govan) Globally, the steel industry is under massive pressure, Among other factors, there’s an almost constant over-supply which keeps prices depressed. After peaking four years ago, the industry’s financial performance has collapsed to historic lows. And towns built to support the industry are feeling the impact. In Newcastle, northern KZN, steel multi-national ArcelorMittal, also known as AMSA, has announced the biggest mass retrenchments in the country’s history. Formerly known as Iscor, the smelter once created thousands of jobs, but it’s now buckling from the pressure of rising electricity costs and cheap steel imports. AMSA is Beeshoek’s only client. (Andrè Joubert) Amsa is the last real steel producer in South Africa and because the economy is not growing, they can’t make steel profitable anymore. Because they can’t make steel profitable, they don’t buy ore from us and we’ve got no other option but to close the mine down. (Govan) Andre Joubert oversees iron ore operations for African Rainbow Minerals, a major shareholder in Beeshoek. He says the mine is preparing for its final shift. (Andrè Joubert) The last 18 months, this mine and the contract with Amsa was a month-on-month contract. And in July, I did not have a contract for August and we still continued to mine in good faith we kept on going. (Govan) In the past four months, the mine has produced nearly 900 THOUSAND tons of ore… but they can’t get it to market. (Govan) Is there a market to sell the ore that you have taken out here? (Andrè Joubert) Absolutely. (Govan) where is that market? (Andrè Joubert) In China. (Govan) what is stopping the access to the market that is over there? (Andrè Joubert) Transnet, I cannot get the ore from here, onto the railway line to Saldana to export. (Adèle Rossouw subtitles) Every time you spot an unfamiliar bakkie outside Beeshoek, you hope it’s a buyer. (Govan) Adèle Rossouw, from the Trade Union, Solidarity, is doing all she can to save jobs at Beeshoek. Adele takes us to a quiet suburb where many of Beeshoek’s miners live. (Adèle Rossouw subtitles) The houses are so beautiful to me, and that’s why I wanted us to stop here, so you can see what the mine did. They helped people become homeowners. The reality is that by December or January, all the families with children in school who have to relocate, there’s going to be a big move-out by the end of the year. (Govan Subtitles) Out of this neighbourhood? It’s such a nice area, kids ride their bikes here. (Adèle Rossouw subtitles) Yes, it’s moms and dads losing their jobs. Those children will have to move and find new schools. (Govan) If that happens, as seems likely, it’ll mean the younger generations will lose a connection to Beeshoek and its legacy. (Adèle Rossouw subtitles) It’s always such a beautiful story for me, when you ask the children here in Postmasburg what they want to be one day, they say, “a multiskilled operator.” It’s so humble such a modest dream. (Govan subtitles) In Postmasburg, being a multiskilled operator is a badge of honour from Beeshoek (Adèle Rossouw subtitles) If we want to be angry, we should channel that anger toward the government. Beeshoek lost its only client, and the reason is total state collapse. Why did Amsa collapse? It’s because of corruption, electricity issues, and all the problems with Transnet. These job losses are a bloodbath. (Leonie Horn subtitles) Everyone is being retrenched, it’s a full retrenchment even I’m being retrenched. We’ve really looked at everything, we’ve tried everything. We even tried things they told us wouldn’t work, but we did it anyway, just so we could say we tried. (Govan) But this is not a community that easily surrenders hope. And there’s no better monument to its fighting spirit than the sports club at the centre of life at the mine. (Wilna Koen Subtitles) When we got the news that things were going to be stopped, I cried at first because I told myself, I don’t k now how I’ll lock the front door behind me for the last time. I’ll fight until the day I walk out of here to make sure this history is preserved, for our children and for those who remain behind. (Adèle Rossouw subtitles) For the next 36 months, if Beeshoek reopens, the people can be called back. (Govan subtitles) Well, at least there’s that. (Adèle Rossouw subtitles) I think that little flame of hope is still burning in everyone’s hearts. (Govan) And as they wait, perhaps they can find inspiration in a team of underdogs who defied the odds to be crowned provincial rugby champions for the first time in more than 50 years.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A town built on iron now stands on hope alone
metadata.Unique Selling Point: As South Africa’s industrial heart falls silent, one small mining community on the edge of the Kalahari faces a reckoning: what happens to a town when the mine that built it begins to fade?
metadata.Summary: On the edge of the Kalahari lies Beeshoek, a mining town built on red earth and iron ore and on the life that grew around its heartbeat, the mine club. For decades, the Ammosal Club was where miners celebrated paydays, children learned to swim, and families gathered under the floodlights after long shifts underground. It was the soul of a community sustained by the mine’s rhythm. Now, that rhythm is faltering. As South Africa’s steel industry declines and ArcelorMittal slows production, Beeshoek’s future and the life built around it hangs in the balance. The ore that once forged the nation’s pride now sails east to feed foreign furnaces, returning as imported steel at a price South Africans can no longer afford.
metadata.Further information: A drone rises above the dust of the Northern Cape. The town of Postmasburg stretches small and thin across the landscape, its streets quiet, its future uncertain. On a map it barely registers, just another dot in a wide, arid land. But for the people who live here, the world has always begun and ended in one place, the Beeshoek mine. For the workers, the mine was more than an employer. It was a father, a constant presence. At sixteen you left school, and your path was already set. Your hands would carry ore, as your father’s had, as your grandfather’s had before him. Generations lined up against the horizon of the pit, their lives defined by shifts and sirens. This is where it began, ninety-nine years ago. A handful of workers and their families, bound together by the earth. The clubhouse became its second heartbeat, established around the rugby club, Ammosal. It became well-known for producing 4 Springbok rugby players, and scores of Griekwa players. The club became the life of the community. It is such a culture, such a core of who they were that the Springboks who came from here, had their ashes scattered on the rugby field. And now, the mine will not turn 100 years old next year. It is closing its doors before Christmas leaving behind generations of families who know no life beyond mining. Their story unfolds against the backdrop of South Africa’s collapsing steel industry. The closure of Beeshoek is not an isolated tragedy, but the symptom of a far wider collapse. South Africa’s government has failed to regulate and protect its steel industry, allowing cheap imports and weak oversight to hollow out local production. At the same time, the collapse of Transnet’s rail network has crippled the movement of ore, forcing mines to rely on costly, inefficient road transport that eats away at margins. Layered over this is Eskom’s spiraling energy crisis: power cuts that stall production, soaring tariffs that push costs beyond viability, and an unreliable grid that makes long-term planning impossible. The story of Postmasburg is therefore more than a community losing its heartbeat, it is a warning of how national policy failure, broken infrastructure, and a failing power utility are dismantling the backbone of South Africa’s industrial economy. Shutdowns & Layoff Plans • AMSA (ArcelorMittal South Africa) is preparing to shut its long steel operations in Newcastle and Vereeniging. • Initially, about 3,500 job cuts were expected from those closures. But unions now warn the cuts could escalate to 4,000 employees, nearly half of AMSA’s workforce, as the layoffs expand to include the Vanderbijlpark flat-steel operations. • In Newcastle, the blast furnace has been placed into care and maintenance, a transitional state often used before full closure. • AMSA had previously deferred the final shutdown to 30 September, backed by funding from the Industrial Development Corporation (IDC).
